hints: Start by sorting the boxes into two groups - those describing amino acid chains and those describing something else in the diagram.
Look at the coiled ribbon shapes labelled F. This is the regular local folding held by hydrogen bonds within one polypeptide.
Compare H which is just the order of amino acids, with G which is the whole 3D folding of one single polypeptide chain.
Now think about J. It describes all four differently shaded polypeptides together as one functional molecule.
For E, recall the small iron-containing non-protein part that actually binds one $O_2$ and gives blood its red colour.
walkthrough:
Remember What Haemoglobin Is Made From**
Haemoglobin is a globular protein with four polypeptide chains, plus four small non-protein groups. Each chain alone is protein, but the oxygen-binding part is not made of amino acids. That is the prosthetic group called haem, with one $Fe^{2+}$ ion that binds one $O_2$. So E is haem.

Link Ribbon Coils to Secondary Structure**
The spiral ribbons you see all over Fig. 4.1 are regular coils within a chain, held by hydrogen bonds between $C=O$ and $N-H$ groups of the backbone. That regular local shape is secondary structure, and the coil type in haemoglobin is the alpha helix. So F is alpha helix.

Separate Sequence From 3D Folding of One Chain**
The simplest level is just the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. That is primary structure, so H is primary structure. When that single chain then folds further by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions into a precise 3D globin, that is tertiary structure, so G is tertiary structure.

Put Four Chains Together**
Haemoglobin only works when two alpha and two beta globins associate together. The arrangement of more than one polypeptide in a functional protein is quaternary structure. So J, the whole molecule of four polypeptides, is quaternary structure.
Final answer: E - haem / prosthetic group; F - alpha helix; G - tertiary structure; H - primary structure; J - quaternary structure.

hints: Blood in the pulmonary veins has just left the lungs, so use the $pCO_2$ 5.3 kPa curve and read up from $pO_2$ 13.0 kPa on the x-axis to the y-axis.
walkthrough:
Choose the Right Curve and Read Across**
Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood away from the lungs where $pCO_2$ is low, so use the left upper curve labelled $pCO_2$ 5.3 kPa. Find $pO_2 = 13.0$ kPa on the x-axis, go straight up to that curve, then straight left to the y-axis. The value is about 98% saturated.
Final answer: 98% saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen.

hints: Compare the two curves in Fig. 4.2 at the same $pO_2$, for example at 4 kPa. Which $pCO_2$ gives lower saturation?
Recall the name given to a rightward shift of the dissociation curve caused by carbon dioxide.
Think about what respiring muscle produces and what happens when $CO_2$ joins with water inside red blood cells.
Link the extra $H^+$ ions to haemoglobin itself and to how tightly haemoglobin can then hold $O_2$.
walkthrough:
State the Effect Seen on the Graph**
At any given $pO_2$, the 10.7 kPa $pCO_2$ curve lies to the right and lower than the 5.3 kPa curve. For example at $pO_2$ 4 kPa saturation is about 60% at low $CO_2$ but only about 45% at high $CO_2$. This rightward shift is the Bohr shift. It means haemoglobin gives up oxygen more readily.

Connect to Strenuous Exercise in Muscle**
Actively respiring muscle produces much $CO_2$, raising tissue $pCO_2$. That is exactly what the lower curve models. So in exercising muscle, for the same low tissue $pO_2$, haemoglobin saturation falls and oxygen dissociates to supply the muscle.

Explain the Chemistry Behind Lower Affinity**
$CO_2$ diffuses into red blood cells and reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates to release $H^+$ ions. The $H^+$ ions are taken up by haemoglobin, forming haemoglobinic acid. This changes haemoglobin shape and greatly decreases its affinity for oxygen, so $O_2$ is released where it is most needed.

Final answer: Bohr shift / Bohr effect. Higher $pCO_2$ shifts curve right, lowering % saturation at same $pO_2$ so more $O_2$ dissociates. Increased $CO_2$ forms carbonic acid, increasing $H^+$ ions which bind to haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid, reducing haemoglobin affinity for oxygen.
